doc.title: Ronnie Zito interviewed by Monk Rowe & Rick Montalbano, via Zoom, March 9, 2022

title: Getting into New York studio work in the 1970s
summary: Early work for Pat Williams and Steve Carmen; midtown studios, now gone.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: So Ronnie, did you fall into studio work or was it like I want to get in the studio scene?

Well it wasn’t a thing like I — well when I got married yeah, we settled down and actually I did work for my brother, my brother was doing some stuff. My brother didn’t use me first. Actually one of the first people I worked for was Pat Williams, who my brother and Pat were very close you know. And I started working for Pat. And then I called — the only phone call I ever made to try to get a gig, I called this guy, his name was Steve Carmen. He was — he used to do an act. He did a Harry Belafonte act, guitar and played you know. He worked with Bobby, accompanied Bobby a little bit, this was before I was with Bobby. And he used to say to me, “If you ever come to New York give me a call.” You know. And I called him. I said, “Well Steve, how you doing?” He says, “Hey can you do a recording with me” blah blah blah “next week, we’re doing a film.” A cheap film. They called them nudie films, he was doing nudie films. And so he said, “Can you do this?” I said, “Sure.” Then he started using me man, and he became the hottest jingle writer in New York, bar none man. He was the hottest. And I did all of his work, all of it for years. And then I worked with other people. You know I was working with — but he used to call me, his contractor would call me and give me dates way ahead of time. “Hold on to Thursday from 1 to 4; hold on to Tuesday” you know, “from 6 to 9 or something” you know. And he would give me holds and then they’d call in the date when he got it. You know. But he would hold his rhythm section.
So you’d travel from one date to another in a particular day.

Oh yeah we were running man. See and what was great in those days in the 70s in New York was all the studios, most of them were close. You could walk to them. You could walk from one studio to another, or hop in a cab for just five minutes and you’d be at the next studio. You know. Everything was close. Everything was all centered in midtown you know. And then that all ended man. You know there’s no studios left in New York man, I’m telling you, there’s a couple of rehearsal studios. There are no recording studios man. The big rooms, Tony Bennett, the big rooms everybody recorded in, Steve and Eydie recorded, they’re all gone. All those studios are gone man. They tore them down man. And there’s hardly any jingle work anymore. And there used to be a ton of it. I mean I bought my first house man, with residuals. And it was like it just didn’t stop. And I was young, you know, I had a lot of energy. We could run around. But that all ended, man. And then people started taking gigs on Broadway because the bands on Broadway
were not that good in the old days. Now, man, the bands on Broadway are terrific because these guys are out of work, the good players.
So they’re taking gigs, they’re happy to get a Broadway show. Plus you get your pension built up from a Broadway show. You know.
